## The problem

Our team of twelve has drifted into long-lived feature branches, some open for three or four weeks. Merges have become dreaded events: conflicts pile up, integration bugs surface late, and code review turns into an archaeology exercise across hundreds of changed lines instead of a quick check of a small diff. Two releases this quarter slipped because a "final merge" surfaced problems nobody had seen coming. We are paying an integration tax, and it is getting more expensive every sprint.

## The proposal

We should move to trunk-based development: everyone commits small, reviewed changes directly to main at least daily, guarded by feature flags for anything unfinished.

- Branches live no longer than a day or two, ideally just hours.
- Feature flags let us ship incomplete work safely, decoupling deploy from release.
- CI must run on every commit to main, not just at merge time, so main stays releasable.
- Code review shifts to small, fast-turnaround diffs rather than sprawling end-of-branch reviews.
- We adopt a shared checklist for flag hygiene so flags get cleaned up instead of accumulating as debt.

This isn't a tooling change so much as a discipline change, and it will require buy-in from everyone, not just the leads.

## What could go wrong

The strongest objection is real: trunk-based development assumes strong CI and a culture of small commits, and if either is missing, we risk breaking main constantly and blocking the whole team. With twelve engineers all committing to one branch, a bad commit has blast radius immediately, whereas a broken feature branch only hurts its author. This is a legitimate risk, not a strawman — it's why the proposal explicitly pairs the branching change with mandatory pre-merge CI gates and a rollback-first mindset, and why we should pilot it on one workstream before rolling it out team-wide.

We should also expect slower initial velocity as people learn to slice work into flag-gated increments, and some resistance from engineers who like the isolation of a branch. Both are manageable with training and a two-week pilot.

I would like a decision by the end of next week.
